text: And Job took up his discourse again and said:
As God lives, who has denied me justice, as the Almighty lives, who has made my soul bitter—
as long as there is breath in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils,
my lips will speak no wrong, and my tongue will utter no deceit.
Far be it from me to say that you are right; till my last breath I will not let go of my integrity.
I hold fast to my righteousness and will not release it; my heart does not reproach me for any of my days.
Let my enemy be counted as the wicked, and the one who rises against me as the unjust.
For what hope has the godless when he is cut off, when God takes away his life?

versions.text: For what hope has the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life?
versions.explanation: In the first clause the Hebrew verb יִבְצָע has the godless man as its subject ("when he is cut off" or "when he gains by violence"); God is named only in the second clause. Naming God as the agent in both clauses adds words not in the text and blunts the parallelism.

text: Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?
Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?
I will teach you about the hand of God; what is with the Almighty I will not conceal.
Look, all of you have seen it for yourselves; why then do you go on with such empty talk?
This is the portion a wicked man receives from God, the inheritance that tyrants get from the Almighty:
If his children increase, it is for the sword, and his offspring will never have bread enough.
Those he leaves behind are buried by the plague, and his widows do not weep for him.
Though he piles up silver like dust and heaps up clothing like clay,
what he heaps up the righteous will wear, and the innocent will divide his silver.
He builds his house like a moth's cocoon, like a shelter a watchman throws together.
He lies down rich, but he will not be gathered; he opens his eyes, and it is gone.

versions.text: He lies down rich, but not for long; he opens his eyes, and everything is gone.
versions.explanation: "But not for long" paraphrases away the Hebrew idiom וְלֹא יֵאָסֵף, "and he is not gathered" (i.e., not gathered to his fathers, left unburied / gone for good). The rendering loses a concrete image of the wicked man's end.

versions.text: He lies down rich, and he is gathered no more; he opens his eyes, and all of it is gone.
versions.explanation: "Gathered no more" can suggest he had been gathered previously and then ceased to be; the Hebrew וְלֹא יֵאָסֵף simply denies that he will be gathered (to his fathers / to burial) at all. "But he will not be gathered" states the idiom cleanly and keeps the contrast with "lies down rich." "All of it" also adds a quantifier not in the terse וְאֵינֶנּוּ; "and it is gone" is shorter and reads better aloud.

text: Terrors overtake him like rushing waters; in the night a whirlwind steals him away.

versions.text: Terrors overtake him like a flood; in the night a storm sweeps him away.
versions.explanation: The verb גָּנַב means "steal, carry off by stealth," which gives the line its force; "sweeps him away" flattens it. Also, כַמַּיִם is literally "like waters," and "rushing waters" keeps the image closer to the Hebrew while still reading naturally aloud.

text: The east wind lifts him up, and he is gone; it hurls him from his place.
It flings itself against him without mercy; he flees headlong from its grip.
It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place.
